q: What is the maximum number of IAM instance profiles you can create per AWS account?

exp.a: Incorrect. The limit is not 500.
exp.b: Correct. The default limit for IAM instance profiles per AWS account is 1000.

q: What is the maximum number of SAML identity providers you can create per AWS account?

exp.a: Incorrect. The limit is not 50.
exp.b: Incorrect. The limit is not 100.
exp.c: Correct. You can create a maximum of 128 SAML identity providers per AWS account.

q: What is the maximum number of OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity providers per AWS account?

exp.a: Incorrect. The limit is not 50.
exp.b: Incorrect. The limit is not 100.
exp.c: Correct. You can create a maximum of 128 OIDC identity providers per AWS account.

q: Which of the following actions can ONLY be performed by the AWS root user?

opts.b: Changing the AWS account name and root user password

exp.a: Incorrect. Any IAM user with appropriate permissions can create IAM users.
exp.b: Correct. Changing the AWS account name, root user email, and root user password are tasks that can only be performed by the root user.
exp.c: Incorrect. Any authorized IAM user can launch EC2 instances.
exp.d: Incorrect. Any authorized IAM user can create S3 buckets.

q: What is the maximum size of an inline policy for an IAM user?

exp.a: Correct. The maximum size of an inline policy for an IAM user is 2,048 characters.
exp.b: Incorrect. 5,120 characters is the limit for inline policies on a group.
exp.c: Incorrect. 6,144 characters is the limit for managed policies.
exp.d: Incorrect. 10,240 characters is the limit for inline policies on a role.

q: What is the maximum size of an inline policy for an IAM group?

exp.a: Incorrect. 2,048 is the limit for users.
exp.b: Correct. The maximum size of an inline policy for an IAM group is 5,120 characters.
exp.d: Incorrect. 10,240 is the limit for roles.

q: What is the maximum size of an inline policy for an IAM role?

exp.a: Incorrect. 2,048 is the limit for users.
exp.b: Incorrect. 5,120 is the limit for groups.
exp.c: Incorrect. 6,144 is the limit for managed policies.
exp.d: Correct. The maximum size of an inline policy for an IAM role is 10,240 characters.

q: Which STS API call is used for web identity federation without using Amazon Cognito?

exp.a: Incorrect. AssumeRole is for general role assumption, not web identity federation.
exp.b: Correct. AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is used to assume a role using web identity tokens from providers like Google, Facebook, or Amazon.
exp.c: Incorrect. AssumeRoleWithSAML is for SAML-based federation.
exp.d: Incorrect. GetFederationToken is for creating temporary credentials for federated users through a custom broker.

q: Which STS API call is used for SAML-based enterprise federation?

exp.a: Incorrect. AssumeRole is for general role assumption.
exp.b: Incorrect. AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is for web identity federation.
exp.c: Correct. AssumeRoleWithSAML returns temporary credentials for users authenticated through a SAML 2.0 identity provider.

q: What is the maximum session duration for credentials obtained via sts:GetFederationToken?

exp.a: Incorrect. 1 hour is too short for GetFederationToken.
exp.b: Incorrect. 12 hours is the max for AssumeRole.
exp.c: Correct. The maximum session duration for credentials obtained via GetFederationToken is 36 hours.
exp.d: Incorrect. 72 hours exceeds the allowed maximum.

q: What is the minimum session duration for credentials obtained via sts:AssumeRole?

exp.a: Incorrect. The minimum is not 5 minutes.
exp.b: Correct. The minimum session duration for AssumeRole is 15 minutes (900 seconds).
exp.c: Incorrect. The minimum is shorter than 30 minutes.
exp.d: Incorrect. 1 hour is the default, not the minimum.

q: What is the 'Version' element in an IAM policy used for?

opts.a: To track how many times the policy was edited
opts.b: To specify the IAM policy language version
opts.c: To define the user who created the policy
opts.d: To set the expiry date of the policy

exp.a: Incorrect. Version does not track edits.
exp.b: Correct. The Version element specifies the policy language version. The current version is '2012-10-17'. Using this ensures access to all policy features.
exp.c: Incorrect. Version does not identify the creator.
exp.d: Incorrect. IAM policies do not have expiry dates set by the Version field.

q: Which condition key would you use to restrict access based on the time of the request?

exp.a: Incorrect. aws:SourceIp restricts based on IP address.
exp.b: Correct. aws:CurrentTime is used to restrict access based on the date and time of the request.
exp.c: Incorrect. aws:SecureTransport checks if the request was made using SSL/TLS.
exp.d: Incorrect. aws:PrincipalOrgID checks the organization ID of the requester.

q: What does the condition key 'aws:SecureTransport' check?

opts.a: Whether the request was made from a VPN
opts.b: Whether the request was sent using SSL/TLS (HTTPS)
opts.d: Whether the user is in a specific region

exp.a: Incorrect. This key does not check for VPN usage.
exp.b: Correct. aws:SecureTransport checks whether the request was made using SSL/TLS (HTTPS). Setting it to 'true' ensures encrypted connections.
exp.c: Incorrect. MFA is checked using aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent.
exp.d: Incorrect. Region is checked with aws:RequestedRegion.

q: What is Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) in IAM?

opts.a: A strategy that uses VPC IDs for access control
opts.b: A strategy that defines permissions based on attributes (tags) attached to users and resources
opts.d: A method to create IAM groups

exp.a: Incorrect. ABAC does not use VPC IDs.
exp.b: Correct. ABAC uses tags (attributes) attached to IAM principals and AWS resources to control access. It allows fine-grained permissions that scale dynamically.
exp.c: Incorrect. ABAC is not related to encryption.
exp.d: Incorrect. ABAC is not about creating groups.

q: What is the difference between an IAM user and an IAM role?

opts.a: Users have permanent credentials; roles provide temporary credentials
opts.b: Users are for services; roles are for humans
opts.d: Roles have permanent credentials; users provide temporary credentials

exp.a: Correct. IAM users have permanent long-term credentials (password, access keys). IAM roles provide temporary security credentials when assumed.
exp.b: Incorrect. It's the opposite; users are typically for humans, and roles are often for services.

q: Which AWS service would you use for identity management for mobile and web applications?

exp.a: Incorrect. IAM is for managing access to AWS services, not for application end-users.
exp.b: Correct. Amazon Cognito provides identity management for web and mobile app users, including sign-up, sign-in, and access control.
exp.c: Incorrect. Shield is for DDoS protection.
exp.d: Incorrect. WAF is a web application firewall.

q: What is the maximum number of server certificates you can store in IAM per AWS account?

exp.a: Incorrect. The limit is not 10.
exp.b: Correct. You can store a maximum of 20 server certificates in IAM per AWS account.

q: What does the 'Sid' element in an IAM policy statement represent?

opts.b: Statement ID — an optional identifier for the policy statement
opts.c: Service ID of the AWS service

exp.a: Incorrect. Sid is not a security ID.
exp.b: Correct. Sid (Statement ID) is an optional identifier that you provide for the policy statement. It must be unique within a JSON policy.
exp.c: Incorrect. Sid is not a service identifier.
exp.d: Incorrect. Sid is not a session ID.

q: Which IAM feature helps you implement the principle of least privilege by showing unused permissions?

exp.a: Incorrect. Credential reports show credential status, not unused permissions.
exp.b: Correct. IAM Access Advisor shows when services were last accessed, helping you identify and remove unused permissions to implement least privilege.
exp.c: Incorrect. Policy Simulator tests policies but doesn't show usage history.
exp.d: Incorrect. CloudTrail logs API calls but doesn't directly show unused permissions in the same way.

q: What is the 'NotResource' element in an IAM policy?

opts.b: It explicitly matches every resource EXCEPT those specified
opts.c: It denies access to all resources

exp.a: Incorrect. NotResource does not mean all resources.
exp.b: Correct. NotResource matches every resource except the ones listed. Use it carefully as it can grant broader access than intended.
exp.c: Incorrect. NotResource doesn't inherently deny access.
exp.d: Incorrect. NotResource does not create resources.

q: What is the maximum path length for IAM entities (users, groups, roles)?

exp.a: Incorrect. The path limit is not 128.
exp.b: Incorrect. The path limit is not 256.
exp.c: Correct. The maximum path length for IAM entities is 512 characters.
exp.d: Incorrect. The path limit is not 1024.

q: What AWS feature allows you to set a permission boundary for actions that IAM administrators can delegate?

exp.a: Incorrect. Groups organize users but don't set boundaries.
exp.b: Correct. Permissions Boundaries allow administrators to set the maximum permissions that a user or role can have, preventing privilege escalation.
exp.c: Incorrect. VPC endpoints are for private network access.
exp.d: Incorrect. Security groups are for network traffic control.

q: What is the Access Key ID length in AWS?

exp.a: Incorrect. The Access Key ID is not 16 characters.
exp.b: Correct. The Access Key ID is 20 characters long and begins with AKIA for long-term keys or ASIA for temporary credentials.
exp.c: Incorrect. The Access Key ID is not 32 characters.
exp.d: Incorrect. 40 characters is the length of the Secret Access Key, not the Access Key ID.

q: What is the Secret Access Key length in AWS?

exp.a: Incorrect. 20 characters is the Access Key ID length.
exp.b: Incorrect. The Secret Access Key is not 32 characters.
exp.c: Correct. The Secret Access Key is 40 characters long.
exp.d: Incorrect. The Secret Access Key is not 64 characters.

q: When can you view or download the Secret Access Key for an IAM user?

opts.b: Only at the time of creation

exp.a: Incorrect. The secret key cannot be retrieved after creation.
exp.b: Correct. The Secret Access Key can only be viewed or downloaded at the time it is created. If lost, you must create a new access key.
exp.d: Incorrect. Even the CLI cannot retrieve a previously created secret key.

q: What does the IAM condition key 'aws:RequestedRegion' allow you to do?

opts.a: Encrypt data in a specific region
opts.b: Restrict API calls to specific AWS regions

exp.a: Incorrect. This key doesn't handle encryption.
exp.b: Correct. aws:RequestedRegion allows you to restrict which AWS regions users can make API calls to, useful for data residency requirements.
exp.c: Incorrect. This key restricts, not enables, regional access.
exp.d: Incorrect. Cost monitoring is done through Cost Explorer.

q: Which API call is used to get temporary credentials for an IAM user with MFA?

exp.a: Incorrect. AssumeRole is for assuming roles, not getting session tokens with MFA.
exp.b: Correct. sts:GetSessionToken is typically used when an IAM user needs temporary credentials with MFA authentication for API access.
exp.c: Incorrect. AssumeRoleWithSAML is for SAML federation.
exp.d: Incorrect. CreateLoginProfile creates a console password.

q: What is the purpose of an IAM path?

opts.b: To organize IAM entities and provide a way to structure them hierarchically
opts.c: To define the order of policy evaluation

exp.a: Incorrect. Paths are not related to network routing.
exp.b: Correct. IAM paths allow you to organize IAM users, groups, and roles in a hierarchical structure (e.g., /division/department/team/) for easier management.
exp.c: Incorrect. Policy evaluation order is not determined by paths.
exp.d: Incorrect. VPC peering is unrelated to IAM paths.

q: What is the maximum number of signing certificates per IAM user?

exp.a: Incorrect. Users can have more than 1.
exp.b: Correct. Each IAM user can have a maximum of 2 signing certificates (X.509 certificates).

q: IAM users can belong to multiple IAM groups.

exp.a: Correct. An IAM user can belong to up to 10 IAM groups simultaneously.
exp.b: Incorrect. IAM users can belong to multiple groups (up to 10).

q: IAM groups can be nested inside other IAM groups.

exp.a: Incorrect. IAM groups cannot contain other groups; they can only contain users.
exp.b: Correct. IAM groups cannot be nested. Groups can only contain IAM users, not other groups.

q: An IAM policy can be attached directly to an AWS resource like an S3 bucket.

exp.a: Correct. Resource-based policies (like S3 bucket policies) can be attached directly to AWS resources.
exp.b: Incorrect. Resource-based policies exist and can be directly attached to resources.

q: The root account can be restricted by Service Control Policies (SCPs) in an AWS Organization member account.

exp.a: Correct. SCPs can restrict the root user in member accounts of an AWS Organization (but not in the management/master account).
exp.b: Incorrect. SCPs do apply to root users in member accounts.

q: IAM roles have permanent access keys associated with them.

exp.a: Incorrect. Roles do not have permanent credentials; they provide temporary security credentials.
exp.b: Correct. IAM roles do not have permanent access keys. When a role is assumed, AWS STS provides temporary credentials.

q: An explicit Deny in an IAM policy can be overridden by an explicit Allow in another policy.

exp.a: Incorrect. An explicit Deny can never be overridden by an Allow.
exp.b: Correct. An explicit Deny always takes precedence over any Allow in IAM policy evaluation. This is a fundamental rule.

q: IAM is a regional service, meaning users created in one region are not available in another.

exp.a: Incorrect. IAM is a global service.
exp.b: Correct. IAM is a global service. Users, groups, roles, and policies are available across all AWS regions.

q: AWS charges a monthly fee for using the IAM service.

exp.a: Incorrect. IAM is free of charge.
exp.b: Correct. AWS IAM is provided at no additional charge. You only pay for other AWS services accessed by your IAM users.

q: A permissions boundary grants permissions to an IAM user.

exp.a: Incorrect. Permissions boundaries do not grant permissions.
exp.b: Correct. A permissions boundary only sets the maximum permissions an entity can have. It does not grant any permissions on its own. Permissions must still be granted through identity-based policies.

q: You can use IAM tags to implement Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC).

exp.a: Correct. IAM tags can be used in policy conditions to implement ABAC, allowing dynamic permissions based on matching tags between principals and resources.
exp.b: Incorrect. ABAC with tags is a supported and recommended strategy in AWS.

q: An IAM user can have both console access and programmatic access at the same time.

exp.a: Correct. An IAM user can be configured with both a password for console access and access keys for programmatic access simultaneously.
exp.b: Incorrect. Both types of access can be enabled for the same user.

q: The Secret Access Key can be retrieved from the IAM console after it has been created.

exp.a: Incorrect. The Secret Access Key cannot be retrieved after creation.
exp.b: Correct. The Secret Access Key is only shown once at the time of creation. If lost, you must delete the old key and create a new one.

q: IAM Access Analyzer can identify resources shared with external entities outside your AWS account.

exp.a: Correct. IAM Access Analyzer identifies resources (like S3 buckets, IAM roles, KMS keys) that are shared with external entities, helping you detect unintended access.
exp.b: Incorrect. This is exactly what Access Analyzer does.

q: Service Control Policies (SCPs) can grant permissions to IAM users.

exp.a: Incorrect. SCPs cannot grant permissions.
exp.b: Correct. SCPs only define the maximum available permissions (guardrails). They do not grant permissions. Permissions must still be granted through IAM policies.

q: An IAM role can be assumed by an AWS service like EC2 or Lambda.

exp.a: Correct. AWS services like EC2, Lambda, and others can assume IAM roles to obtain temporary credentials for accessing other AWS resources.
exp.b: Incorrect. Service roles are commonly used for AWS services to assume roles.

q: You can attach a managed policy to multiple IAM users, groups, and roles simultaneously.

exp.a: Correct. Managed policies are standalone policies that can be attached to multiple users, groups, and roles. This is one of their key advantages over inline policies.
exp.b: Incorrect. Reusability across entities is the primary benefit of managed policies.

q: The IAM credential report can be generated in CSV format.

exp.a: Correct. The IAM credential report is generated and downloaded in CSV (Comma Separated Values) format.
exp.b: Incorrect. The credential report is indeed in CSV format.

q: IAM policies can be written in YAML format.

exp.a: Incorrect. IAM policies must be in JSON format.
exp.b: Correct. IAM policies can only be written in JSON format. While CloudFormation templates support YAML, IAM policy documents themselves must be JSON.

q: An IAM group is an identity that can be used to authenticate to AWS.

exp.a: Incorrect. Groups are not identities that can authenticate.
exp.b: Correct. An IAM group is not an identity and cannot be used to authenticate. It is simply a collection of IAM users for easier permission management. You cannot log in as a group.

q: By default, all requests in AWS are implicitly denied unless explicitly allowed.

exp.a: Correct. By default, all requests are implicitly denied. An explicit Allow in a policy is required to grant access (except for the root user).
exp.b: Incorrect. The default behavior in AWS is implicit deny.

q: You can use IAM to configure multi-factor authentication for the AWS root account.

exp.a: Correct. MFA can and should be enabled for the root account. This is an AWS security best practice.
exp.b: Incorrect. MFA is fully supported for the root account.

q: IAM supports identity federation using SAML 2.0.

exp.a: Correct. AWS IAM supports SAML 2.0-based federation, allowing users from enterprise identity providers to access AWS resources.
exp.b: Incorrect. SAML 2.0 federation is fully supported by IAM.

q: An IAM user can assume an IAM role in the same AWS account.

exp.a: Correct. IAM users can assume roles within the same account if the role's trust policy allows it and the user has permission to call sts:AssumeRole.
exp.b: Incorrect. Same-account role assumption is a common and supported practice.

q: Inline policies are automatically deleted when the associated IAM entity is deleted.

exp.a: Correct. Inline policies are embedded directly in the entity. When the user, group, or role is deleted, the inline policy is also deleted.
exp.b: Incorrect. Inline policies have a one-to-one relationship with their entity and are deleted with it.

q: You can use the IAM Policy Simulator to test policies without actually making real API calls to AWS services.

exp.a: Correct. The IAM Policy Simulator simulates the effect of policies without making actual API calls. It helps you test and debug permissions.
exp.b: Incorrect. The Policy Simulator does not make real API calls; it only simulates policy evaluation.

q: The Principal element is required in identity-based IAM policies.

exp.a: Incorrect. The Principal element is not used in identity-based policies.
exp.b: Correct. The Principal element is NOT included in identity-based policies because the principal is implicitly the entity (user, group, role) the policy is attached to. Principal is used in resource-based policies and trust policies.

q: AWS recommends using access keys for the root account for automation tasks.

exp.a: Incorrect. AWS strongly recommends against creating access keys for the root account.
exp.b: Correct. AWS best practice is to never create access keys for the root account. Instead, create IAM users or roles with appropriate permissions for automation.

q: A customer managed policy can be shared across multiple AWS accounts directly.

exp.a: Incorrect. Customer managed policies cannot be directly shared across accounts.
exp.b: Correct. Customer managed policies are specific to an AWS account and cannot be directly shared with other accounts. You would need to recreate them in each account or use AWS Organizations.

q: An IAM role can have both a permissions policy and a trust policy.

exp.a: Correct. Every IAM role has two types of policies: a trust policy (defines who can assume the role) and permissions policies (define what the role can do once assumed).
exp.b: Incorrect. Roles always have both a trust policy and one or more permissions policies.
